Triggers.value: Feeling physically restrained or held down

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Going to or near the place where the event happened
I try hard to control my emotions

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
issues.explanation: These triggers are hard to reconcile with the stated trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner. 'Feeling restrained or held down' fits well, but medical equipment and helicopter sounds suggest a medical, combat, or accident context that is not represented in the Threat, Memory, Appraisals, or Strategy items.

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
issues.explanation: Because Triggers has strong links to Threat and Memory in the formulation, the trigger content should plausibly connect to the patient's danger cues and trauma memories. The profile's Threat items center on interpersonal hypervigilance in close environments (silence, nearby movement, lock checking), and Memory items do not contain medical or aircraft content, making these two triggers clinically incoherent with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
issues.explanation: 'Helicopter or aircraft sounds' is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type of physical abuse by a romantic partner unless there is additional undisclosed trauma exposure; it does not fit the rest of the profile, which centers on interpersonal/domestic threat cues such as restraint, doors, movement, and lock checking.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
issues.explanation: 'Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen' is not impossible, but paired with the otherwise specifically interpersonal/domestic cue pattern it weakens coherence because it suggests a different threat context without support from memory or appraisal items.

vignette:
Javier Morales is a 37-year-old Latino man who came to treatment after months of telling himself he should be able to handle things on his own. He works in social ministry, visiting families, helping coordinate church-based assistance, and spending long hours in parish offices and apartment buildings across the city. He is divorced now, and when he speaks about the relationship that ended, he does so with a flat effortful composure that can suddenly give way to silence. The traumatic event he returns to most often happened late at night in the apartment he once shared with his former partner, after she had been drinking. He remembers the smell before anything else: alcohol on her breath and in the room, sharp and sour, mixed with the stale air of the apartment. What remains clearest is how quickly the argument became physical. When he tried to step away, she shoved him back onto the bed, held him down with both hands and the weight of her body, and he could not get free. In his memory he hears the bedroom door slam and then later the apartment door jerk open hard enough to hit the wall. Even now those sounds return with startling force, as if they are happening again rather than being remembered.

In the weeks after he left, Javier found that the event stayed unusually sharp in his mind. He did not describe it as fuzzy or dreamlike; if anything, he hated how exact it was. He could picture the room, the pressure of being pinned, the angle of the light, the smell of liquor, and he could hear in his head the slam of the door and the sudden opening of it. When the memory came, what overtook him was not only fear but grief so intense it embarrassed him. He would think not just of being hurt, but of the collapse of the life he thought he had, and that grief could stop him in the middle of the day. He had come to believe that if he let himself feel too much, he would lose control completely, so he began working hard to keep himself contained. In sessions he describes this almost as a discipline: steady voice, straight posture, no tears if he can help it. He is careful with his expression around other people too, especially in church settings where others come to him for calm.

His daily life narrowed around what felt dangerous. He will not go near the apartment complex where the assault happened, even when a ministry errand in that neighborhood would be convenient. He reroutes himself and makes excuses to coworkers. At work, doors are hard for him. A parish office door swinging open unexpectedly, or a heavy church door slamming in a draft, can make his whole body react before he has time to think. If someone moves suddenly near him in a hallway, he jerks as if bracing for an attack. When he feels threatened, he does not argue or push back; he goes still. He describes freezing completely, his mind going blank while his body waits. This has happened during tense interactions with clients' family members and once when a colleague touched his shoulder from behind in a cramped storage room. He stood there unable to respond, then later acted as though nothing had happened.

Night is the hardest time. Javier checks the locks on his doors and windows repeatedly before bed, then often gets up to check again. He knows the apartment is secure, but he does not feel secure, especially after dark. He listens for movement in the hall and startles at small noises. If he catches the smell of alcohol on a passing stranger in his building or on someone he is serving at an evening outreach event, his chest tightens immediately and his attention locks onto exits, doorways, and who is standing where. He feels ashamed of how quickly this happens, particularly because his work asks him to be present with people in distress, not guarded against them.

Over time these habits have begun to cost him. He has avoided certain home visits, stayed away from evening meetings, and become known among coworkers as unusually controlled and hard to read. Friends from church have noticed that he leaves early from gatherings where drinks are present. What finally brought him to seek help was a recent incident at work when a door slammed behind him in a parish office and he froze in front of a family who had come for assistance. He was humiliated by their concern and shaken by how immediate it felt. Sitting in treatment now, Javier says he is tired of living as if danger is always about to enter through a door. What frightens him most is the idea that this will remain the shape of his life-vigilant at night, avoiding parts of the city, going rigid when startled. What he hopes for, though he says it cautiously, is to remember what happened without hearing it all over again and without feeling that his whole body is still pinned in that room.
